title: Candle Inclusion
summary: Merging candles that “swallow” each other whole — the first step to reading any Chan chart
body:
Here's something easy to miss but that Chan handles first: sometimes one day's high and low completely swallow the day before (or after) it.

Example: say a stock trades between $30 and $36 on Monday, then between $31 and $34 on Tuesday — Tuesday's whole range sits inside Monday's, never poking outside it. That's called an **inclusion relationship**.

When this happens, it's genuinely hard to tell which day was the real high and which was the real low, and that fuzziness would carry into every later step. So the very first thing Chan does is **merge these overlapping candles into one**, and treats them as a single bigger candle from then on.

Which direction they merge depends on **the trend heading into that pair** of candles: if price was rising beforehand, the merged candle takes the higher of the two highs and the higher of the two lows; if price was falling, it takes the lower of both. It's about which way things were going *before* this pair — not which way the merged result points — and that's the part people get backwards.

Everything covered later — fractals, strokes, segments — is built on top of this merged sequence. The chart still shows the original candles, but the structure lines are drawn on the merged result, so a line's endpoint can occasionally look like it doesn't quite line up with a candle's wick. That's normal.

**How this app does it**

This step is now handled automatically by the open-source Chan engine we plug into (**czsc**), following the exact rule above.

Prices are always **split- and dividend-adjusted** before any of this runs — in plain terms, we smooth out the price jump a dividend or bonus share issue would otherwise create, so it doesn't get mistaken for a real structural move.

The chart still shows the original candles; the earliest stretch of data, before the first stroke has even formed, doesn't take part in any of this — nothing to worry about there.

title: Fractal
summary: A local high or low made of three candles — the two endpoints of a stroke
body:
A fractal is the smallest building block in Chan, made of **three consecutive** (merged) candles, and it marks a local high or low in the price path.

**Top fractal** (a local high): the middle candle's high is the highest of the three, *and* its low is also the highest of the three.

**Bottom fractal** (a local low): the middle candle's low is the lowest of the three, *and* its high is also the lowest of the three.

Example: say a stock closes around $32, then $48, then $34 on three straight days — if the middle day ($48) has both the highest high *and* the highest low of the three, that's a top fractal, hinting this may be a short-term peak. Both conditions have to hold *together*: a candle with just the highest high, but not the highest low, doesn't count — that detail is exactly what makes a fractal trustworthy.

A fractal by itself is **not a trade signal**. It's only a candidate turning point; whether it actually holds depends on whether a stroke forms after it (next lesson). On the chart, top fractals are red and bottom fractals green — they mark structure, not “buy here.”

In practice fractals get voided all the time: a bottom fractal forms, the very next candle makes a new low, and that fractal is gone. Anything not yet confirmed by later price is drawn with a dashed line.

**How this app does it**

This step is also handled by the **czsc** engine, using the exact definition above.

The chart **only marks fractals that actually became a stroke endpoint** — candidate fractals that never produced a stroke can be voided at any moment, and drawing them all would just clutter the chart and make it harder to read. Structure at the right edge that later candles haven't confirmed yet is marked “pending.”

title: Stroke
summary: A line from one local high to one local low (or back) — the first structure in Chan with a direction
body:
A stroke connects an adjacent top fractal and bottom fractal — it's the **first structure in Chan that actually has a direction**: up or down.

Continuing the fractal example: if that $48 top fractal is followed by price sliding down to around $34 and forming a bottom fractal there, connecting those two points is **one down-stroke**.

Two conditions have to hold:

• The two endpoints must be one top and one bottom, opposite directions
• The two fractals **can't sit too close together** — there needs to be a certain number of candles between them, or the tiniest wobble would draw a stroke and the chart would turn into noise

That second condition is the important one — it's what filters out “price flicked back and forth for a day and reversed” from counting as a real move.

Strokes point up or down: bottom fractal to top fractal is an up-stroke, the reverse is a down-stroke. They're drawn in blue.

**Strokes can disappear.** If price later makes a new high or low, the original fractal endpoint gets overturned, and the stroke built on it changes along with it. That's why the rightmost stroke on the chart is usually dashed — it hasn't been locked in by later price yet, and could still stretch further.

**How this app does it**

Strokes are also computed by the **czsc** engine: the two endpoint fractals can't share a candle, and in practice there need to be at least **6** merged candles between them; the two fractals' price ranges also can't overlap each other.

A stroke's endpoint is whichever fractal after the start went **furthest**: the highest top for an up-stroke, the lowest bottom for a down-stroke. As long as price keeps making new highs or lows, the last stroke keeps **stretching** to match — which is why the last stroke on the chart is always treated as pending.

title: Segment
summary: At least three strokes with overlapping price ranges — a bigger, steadier structure
body:
A stroke is the smallest directional unit, but it can flip back and forth easily; a segment is the next level up that organizes strokes together, filtering out that back-and-forth noise into something far steadier.

Example: if a stock rallies one stroke, pulls back one stroke, then rallies again, and those three strokes' price ranges overlap each other (say all weaving between $40 and $55), that can form a segment — a reasonably stable uptrend, not just a few days of tug-of-war. **A segment needs at least three strokes**, and those strokes need overlapping ranges — three strokes with zero overlap is just a straight one-way move, not a segment.

Deciding when a segment ends is one of the fiddlier parts of Chan: in short, it comes down to whether the move in the opposite direction is “strong” enough to form a new turning point of its own (the technical name is a fractal in the “characteristic sequence” — you don't need to remember that term, just the idea). When it's not obvious, the app looks a few strokes further ahead before concluding, so segments aren't cut off too early. A segment also never swallows its own starting point — once price reclaims where the segment began, that segment needs to be re-examined.

Just remember what a segment is *for*: **it's noise reduction for strokes.** Strokes can flip several times a day; segments are far steadier, and pivots (next lesson) are defined at this level.

Segments are drawn in orange, a bit thicker than the blue strokes. When reading a chart, check the segment direction first, then the stroke detail — doing it backwards makes it easy to get shaken out by short-term noise.

**How this app does it**

A segment is made of at least **3 strokes**, and takes its direction from the first one: a rising first stroke makes an up-segment, a falling one a down-segment. When deciding if a segment has ended, the app looks a few strokes further ahead before confirming, so segments aren't cut short; a segment also **never crosses back over its own starting point**. The most recent segment is marked “pending” until later price action confirms it.

title: Pivot
summary: The overlapping range of several consecutive moves — the core of telling a range from a trend
body:
A pivot can be thought of as **the price zone where buyers and sellers are stuck in a standoff, going back and forth without either side winning** — it's the most central idea in Chan theory.

Example: say a stock spends three rounds bouncing between $58 and $64 (up a stroke to around $64, down a stroke to around $58, back up toward $64…). That $58–$64 overlapping range is a pivot — it tells you that at this price level, neither buyers nor sellers have a clear edge.

A pivot matters because it **marks out a balance zone between bulls and bears**. Price moving in and out of it means there isn't much disagreement; once price leaves and doesn't come back, one side has taken control. That gives two basic outcomes:

• **Range**: just one pivot, with price repeatedly moving in and out of it — like the example above, if the stock never manages to hold above $64
• **Trend**: two or more pivots in the same direction, each one completely clearing the one before it — say the stock later runs all the way to $75 and never falls back below $64, which means the range is over and a trend has taken hold

Pivots are drawn as purple boxes on the chart. **Whether a pivot actually gets broken, and whether a pullback confirms that break, matters more than staring at any single buy or sell point.**

**How this app does it**

Pivots are computed by the **czsc** engine at the stroke level: starting from some stroke, consecutive strokes whose prices overlap get grouped together, and a group needs **at least 3 strokes** to count as a pivot. The pivot's upper bound is the lowest of the first three strokes' highs, and the lower bound is the highest of their lows — and that range **stays fixed** from then on; as the pivot extends, only its overall highest and lowest points get updated. Once price leaves the pivot, if the move back in the opposite direction can't reach the pivot range (it should have broken down but didn't, or should have broken out but didn't), that group of the pivot is done and a new one starts.

Whether the overall move counts as a trend or a range, this app judges purely from **stroke-level pivots** — if you want to see the next degree up, just switch the timeframe to weekly (more on this in “Trend Levels”), rather than the app computing some separate “higher-level” pivot on the same timeframe.

title: Divergence
summary: Price makes a new high (or low), but the push behind it has gotten weaker — a hint not to chase
body:
Divergence is when a move **makes a new high (or low)**, but the **force driving it has actually shrunk** — like a car that's still rolling forward but is visibly running out of gas.

Example: say a stock runs from $50 to $70 (the first leg up), pulls back, then pushes on to a new high of $75 (the second leg up). If that second leg climbed more slowly, on lower volume, and took less time than the first, then even though price did make a new high, that push is likely close to spent — that's divergence.

Two common ways people gauge the force behind a move:

• Compare the area under the MACD histogram for two same-direction legs (the later leg's area is clearly smaller than the earlier one's)
• Just look at speed — is the later leg moving more slowly than the earlier one

This app takes a third approach — directly comparing the **price range, volume, and time taken** of a leg against the prior same-direction leg; the smaller the ratio, the weaker that leg is.

A divergence comparison has to be between two legs of the **same degree, same direction, with a move in between** — comparing two arbitrary legs means nothing.

**Divergence is not a reversal.** It only tells you the current direction has run out of steam — what happens next could genuinely be a reversal, or it could just be sideways consolidation before continuing the same way. Its real value is warning you “don't chase here,” not “flip your position here.”

**How this app does it**

Divergence gets used in two places:

• **Deciding whether a type-1 buy/sell exists**: look at the last 5 to 21 strokes — the first stroke sits at the high of the stretch (the low, for a sell), the last stroke makes a new low (new high, for a sell), and that last stroke's **price range** is weaker than the earlier decline, with **volume or duration** also weaker on at least one count. Only then has the move genuinely run out of force.
• **How strong the divergence is**: by the price-range ratio (this leg's move ÷ the benchmark leg): **under 0.6 is strong, 0.6–0.8 is medium, anything else is weak**. Signal cards show the exact range, volume, and duration ratios; wherever a divergence shows up on the candlestick chart, a solid pink line connects the ends of the two legs being compared, labeled with the range ratio.

The app **doesn't use MACD to judge divergence** — and as a practical simplification, it doesn't strictly require a pivot in between the two legs being compared. If two or more pivots have already formed before the current stroke, it counts as a “trend divergence”; otherwise, a “range divergence,” which is somewhat less reliable.

title: MACD (the most common divergence tool)
summary: Many people use it to gauge divergence strength — but it's not native to Chan, and this app doesn't use it either
body:
**MACD** isn't a concept native to Chan, but a lot of people use it to **quantify how strong a divergence is** — it's the most common tool for the job. Consider this lesson background knowledge (this app actually judges divergence with the “force ratio” approach from the previous lesson).

MACD has three parts:

• **DIF** (blue line): the gap between a fast and a slow moving average, showing how far short-term price has drifted from medium-term
• **DEA** (orange line): a moving average of DIF itself — smoother and slower to react than DIF
• **The histogram**: DIF minus DEA — positive values draw red bars, negative values draw green ones

The bars are the most intuitive part: **longer bars mean the current direction is accelerating; shorter bars (even if still red) mean it's decelerating**; bars crossing from red to green (or back) mean short-term momentum has likely flipped.

Note that shrinking bars do **not** mean the price is falling — they only mean the rise is losing steam. Price still making new highs while the bars are already shrinking is the textbook shape of a divergence.

A lot of people sum up the MACD histogram's area for two same-direction legs and compare them (later divided by earlier) — that ratio is the commonly cited “area ratio”: below 1 means the later leg is weaker, and the smaller it is, the clearer the divergence; near or above 1 means force hasn't actually faded, so it's not a divergence. This comparison also needs two legs of the same degree, same direction, with a move in between — a number from two random legs means nothing.

**MACD is only a measuring tool, not a trade signal.** Shrinking bars only say the current direction is losing force — whether it reverses or just pauses and continues afterward, MACD alone can't tell you.

**How this app does it**

This app **does not use MACD to judge divergence**. The reason: divergence and type-1 buy/sell points need to be judged with **the same yardstick** to make sense together — type-1 signals look at a stroke's force (price range, volume, time taken), so divergence strength is measured with the exact same numbers.

The MACD panel under the analysis chart is kept around for reference, but what actually decides a divergence is the **solid pink line on the candlestick chart**: it connects the ends of the two legs being compared and labels the exact range ratio (e.g. “Top div 0.52”).

title: The Three Buy/Sell Points
summary: Chan groups timing into three types — the further along, the more certain, but also the pricier
body:
Chan groups buy points into three types; sell points follow the exact mirror logic (decline — bounce — decline again).

Here's one running example: say a stock falls from $100 to around $70, bounces around there a few times and forms a pivot, then falls again to $60 — but this last leg down is clearly slower and weaker than the ones before it (that's the divergence from the last lesson). That low around $60 is the **1st buy**: theoretically the bottom, but also the hardest to trust — that “running out of steam” call can be overturned by an even deeper drop at any time, and 1st-buy failures are common.

Price bounces from $60 to $75, pulls back again, but this time only down to $65 — **without breaking below $60**. That point is the **2nd buy**: one more confirmation than the 1st buy (no new low), so lower risk, at the cost of a higher entry price.

Price later breaks above that earlier pivot around $70 and runs to $90, pulls back to $82, and **doesn't fall back into the pivot**. That point is the **3rd buy**: by now the uptrend is basically confirmed — the highest certainty of the three, but already a long way from the original bottom.

At heart, the three buy points are **a trade-off between certainty and price**: the 1st buy is cheap but uncertain, the 3rd buy is solid but expensive.

This app's signal screens show the buy/sell points it detects, which type each one is, and how strong it is. **These are the results of structure detection, not investment advice** — the same spot can be an opposite signal at a different degree, and which degree matters depends on how long you plan to hold.

**How this app does it**

Signals follow the original Chan-theory definitions strictly:

• **1st buy/sell**: must be a **trend divergence** — price has already formed two non-overlapping pivots stepping lower (higher for a sell), then leaves the latest one to make a new low with weaker force than the previous leg. A divergence inside a range (a consolidation divergence) is not labeled as type 1.
• **2nd buy/sell**: the **first retest** after a 1st buy that does not break its low (the first pullback after a 1st sell that does not break its high). Later retests don't count.
• **3rd buy/sell**: a stroke starts inside a pivot and closes outside it (leaving the pivot), and the **first retest** afterwards does not fall back into the pivot (for a sell: the first pullback does not rise back in).

The app adds strength grading on top of that:

• **1st buy/sell**: identified with the force rule from the Divergence lesson, banded by the range ratio (below 0.6 strong, 0.6–0.8 medium, else weak), with the card showing the exact range, volume, and duration ratios.
• **2nd/3rd buy/sell**: strength depends on how solid the most recently completed pivot before this signal was, and how far the pullback landed from the pivot's edge.

Every signal is judged **candle by candle, using only the data available at that moment**, and placed at the end of its stroke. If that stroke later stretches because price kept making new lows or highs, the original signal is treated as void and stops showing.

title: Trend Levels
summary: Level comes from how pivots nest inside each other, not from whether you're on daily or weekly candles — the most common mix-up
body:
Level is the single most misunderstood idea in Chan.

**Level isn't the same thing as candle timeframe.** A daily chart can show a fairly small-degree move, while a 5-minute chart can occasionally trace out a large-degree structure. Level is actually set by **how pivots nest inside each other**: a pivot made of strokes is one level, a pivot made of bigger structures is the next level up, and so on recursively.

In practice, most people approximate level using candle timeframe, because it's convenient:

• 5-min / 30-min — roughly, intraday trading
• Daily — roughly, a swing of days to weeks
• Weekly — roughly, a medium-to-long-term hold

This approximation is good enough most of the time — just remember it's an approximation, not the actual definition.

The real point of level is helping you **decide which layer's signals to actually watch**. For example: a daily-level 1st buy might just be one small piece of a much bigger down-leg on the 30-minute chart; a 30-minute 3rd buy, on the other hand, might not mean anything at all on the daily.

**A signal has to match how long you actually plan to hold.** Using a 5-minute buy point for a months-long hold, or a weekly buy point for same-day trading, is using the right tool in the wrong place. Switching between daily and weekly in this app is exactly switching this layer.

**How this app does it**

The analysis page switches between **daily and weekly**, with weekly candles built from daily ones — if you want to see the next degree up, just switch to weekly, rather than the app computing some separate “higher-level” pivot on the same timeframe.

Within a single timeframe, **the last stroke's direction** stands for the short-term rhythm, and **the segment's direction** stands for the bigger trend; the pattern read-out gives the segment direction more weight.

So the structure doesn't shift depending on which start date happens to be picked, the app pulls in extra history before the range you're viewing and computes over the whole series (roughly 180 days for daily, 540 for weekly), then only shows you the part you're actually looking at.
